title: Boléro
hook: One rhythm, two tunes and fifteen minutes of crescendo. Then the floor gives way.

painting.title: El Jaleo
painting.pairingNote: A dancer in a Spanish tavern, lit from below and egged on by guitars and clapping hands, the scene Boléro was first staged in.

facts: The dancer Ida Rubinstein commissioned a ballet score from Ravel in 1928. He first planned to orchestrate piano pieces by Albéniz, ran into a copyright problem, and decided to write something new instead.
His plan, as he told a friend at the piano: take one insistent tune, repeat it many times without developing it, and make the orchestra grow, step by step.
It was first danced at the Paris Opéra on 22 November 1928. The scenario: a tavern in Spain, a woman dancing on a long table, the crowd growing more excited. Ravel himself imagined a factory.

A snare drum plays the same two-bar rhythm 169 times. Above it, two melodies take turns, each passed to a new instrument or combination. Everything stays in C major until a few seconds before the end.
Ravel called it an experiment and expected orchestras to refuse it. It became his most famous piece.
bigPicture.inOneLine: one rhythm, two tunes, one long [[crescendo|crescendo]].

movements.heading: Boléro
movements.summary: A single, unbroken [[crescendo|crescendo]] from almost nothing to the full orchestra. The rhythm never changes and the tunes never develop; what changes is who plays them. Listen to it as a parade of instrumental colours.

mainIdeas.name: The rhythm
mainIdeas.description: a two-bar pattern on the snare drum, the [[ostinato|ostinato]] that runs from the first bar to the last.

mainIdeas.name: Tune A
mainIdeas.description: smooth and even, it winds down through an octave.

mainIdeas.name: Tune B
mainIdeas.description: more sultry, with bluesy, bent notes and off-beat accents ([[syncopation|syncopation]]); it sinks through two octaves.

stops.hear: A snare drum, barely audible, and soft plucked violas and cellos; after a few seconds a flute enters, low and quiet
stops.happening: The rhythm, then Tune A on the flute

stops.hear: A clarinet plays the same tune
A bassoon, high in its range, with a new, slinkier tune; then the same tune on a small, shrill clarinet
stops.happening: Tune B enters, then repeats on the E-flat clarinet

stops.hear: A [[muted|muted]] trumpet, with a flute shadowing it high above
stops.happening: Tune A in a new colour

stops.hear: A tenor saxophone, then a soprano saxophone, slide through Tune B
stops.happening: The saxophones, a jazz-age touch in 1928

stops.hear: A horn plays Tune A, but it sounds like an organ stop: celesta and two piccolos double it in other keys
stops.happening: The piccolos reinforce the horn’s natural overtones. A strange, glowing sound

stops.hear: A solo trombone, sliding and swaggering
stops.happening: Tune B on the trombone, a famously exposed solo

stops.hear: For the first time the violins take the melody, with woodwinds
stops.happening: The strings join. From here the sound grows thicker with every repeat

stops.hear: The whole orchestra on Tune B; then, without warning, the music lurches up into a new key, E major
stops.happening: The only change of key in the piece, eight bars long

stops.label: Last 30 seconds
stops.hear: Back in C major; bass drum, cymbals and gong crash in for the first time; trombones slide; the whole orchestra beats out the drum rhythm and collapses

notice: Follow the snare drum, not the tune. It never stops and never changes. Later on, a second snare drum joins in.
At ≈ 6:30, try to hear the piccolos inside the horn sound. They are playing the tune in two other keys at once.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Ravel wanted the tempo to stay the same from the first bar to the last; at a 1930 recording session he stopped the conductor for speeding up near the end. His own recording that year lasts about 15 minutes 50 seconds. Dutoit takes 15:03.

threads.title: Repetition instead of development
threads.body: Ravel said the piece had almost no form, no development and almost no change of key. The interest lies in colour and volume.

threads.title: The orchestra as the subject
threads.body: Each repeat is a lesson in instrumentation: solo, pairs, choirs, then everyone.

threads.title: The release
threads.body: Fifteen minutes in one key make the final swerve to E major feel like an earthquake.
